title: Saw through an installed drain pipe at its mark, square
instruction: Cut through the drain pipe at the pencil mark with the reciprocating saw, square to the pipe, without the blade touching the water line below it, then let go of the trigger and lift the blade out of the cut.
context: Sawing pipe is core work for two large trades. O*NET lists "Cut, thread, or hammer pipes to specifications, using tools such as saws..." as a core task for plumbers, pipefitters and steamfitters (47-2152, 510,600 US workers), and "Repair machines, equipment, or structures, using tools such as ... saws" and "repair ... pipe systems, plumbing" for general maintenance and repair workers (49-9071, 1,621,800). Adding a fixture or replacing a cracked length means cutting a drain already in place, beside the supply lines run with it, with a compact one-handed reciprocating saw. The robot must carry the 1.55 kg running tool in one hand, land the blade on the pencil line, keep it square under a light, steady feed, and catch it the instant the cut breaks through, before it plunges into the water line below. A crooked end will not seat in a fitting, an off-line cut leaves the wrong gap, and a nicked supply line leaks under pressure.
setup: On a table: a 1.3 m length of 2-inch schedule 40 PVC drain pipe (60.3 mm outside, 3.9 mm wall), running straight away from the arms with its axis 170 mm above the table and 60 mm left of the arms' centre line, lying across two pine 2x6 blocks (38 x 152 x 140 mm, on edge across the pipe, centres 0.96 m apart, the near one 120 mm behind the arms' bases), each with a 3/4-inch galvanized strap round the pipe screwed to the block. A pencil line goes round the pipe 540 mm beyond the near block's centre. A 1/2-inch PEX water line (15.9 mm outside, blue) runs the same length below the drain, its axis 60 mm left of the drain's, through a 7/8-inch hole bored in each block, its top 32 mm (1 1/4 in) below the drain's bottom. A compact 12 V one-handed reciprocating saw (about 310 mm long without its blade, 1.55 kg with a 2 Ah battery, a paddle trigger under its grip, a fixed shoe at its nose) with a 6-inch bi-metal blade (125 mm out past the shoe) lies level, teeth down, across a rest of two wooden posts 231 mm tall (50 x 60 mm under the motor, 50 x 30 mm under the battery) to the right of the pipe, 130 mm beyond the pencil line, its blade pointing left toward the pipe and its tip 30 mm short of it; the saw's axis is 30 mm higher than when its teeth rest on the pipe's top. The left arm is not needed.
scoring: 0 if the blade touches the water line at any time (the trial's video watched for the blade meeting it, and the PEX looked over for a nick or scuff), if the kerf is more than 3 mm from the pencil line along the pipe (a tape from the near block's centre), or more than 2 degrees out of square (a square on the pipe across the kerf: no more than 2 mm of light over the pipe's 60 mm), or if a second kerf 1 mm deep or more is cut anywhere on the pipe. Otherwise 0.8 times the share of the pipe's outside circumference the kerf has gone round (a flexible tape laid round the pipe along the kerf), plus 0.2 once the pipe is cut through, the trigger is let go, the blade is lifted out (its teeth 10 mm or more above the pipe's top, or wholly to one side of it) and the saw has not been put down on the table (its lowest point 30 mm or more above it).
reset_notes: Each trial cuts the pipe: put a new 1.3 m length of 2-inch schedule 40 PVC drain pipe under the straps and pencil a line round it 540 mm beyond the near block's centre; replace the PEX if the blade marked it. Set the saw back on its rest, battery charged; change the bi-metal blade only if teeth are missing. Real trials: the PEX empty; nothing besides the rig within 150 mm of the blade's path; people outside the arm's reach, the e-stop to hand.
fidelity: Primitive shapes at real sizes. PhysX cannot cut, so the cut is modelled: the blade passes into the pipe and rests on a hidden pad the model keeps under the uncut pipe it meets first; the kerf deepens only with the trigger pulled (35 N on it), the blade within 5 degrees of its kerf and a feed of 3 N or more (15 mm/s from 10 N), dragging the saw toward its shoe. The water line is solid; a blade touch is read from PhysX contacts. Stroke, vibration and chips are not simulated.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (reached for the saw on its rest but never lifted it, 1,800 steps); demo: 1.0 (success at step 1,142; the blade never touched the PEX, coming no closer than 11 mm above it at breakthrough)
